title: Per-tenant escape hatch & atomic fallback — Dedicated capacity PRD (draft)
content:
Purpose
This doc proposes two complementary mechanisms to improve reliability and predictability for Dedicated customers during sudden demand spikes: 1) a per-tenant Escape Hatch (a configurable, low-friction traffic reroute and rate-reduction mechanism) and 2) an Atomic Fallback primitive that guarantees per-request transactional switching to safe lanes (alternate models/vCPU lanes) with clear telemetry and rollback semantics. This is a product + ops-first design focused on minimizing customer-visible errors while preserving tenant isolation and predictable unit costs.

Problem statement
- Tenants on Dedicated occasionally generate bursts that exceed reserved capacity (microbursts, bot churn, bad client loops). Current strategies (soft quota degrade, global throttling, preemptive eviction) either produce noisy failures or unpredictable latency and cost.
- We need a low-latency mechanism to reduce tail error rates without heavy infra changes or long dev cycles.
- Existing ideas (burst credits, warm pools, island routing) handle steady/longer bursts but struggle with short, high-amplitude spikes and with preserving per-tenant isolation contracts.

Goals
- Reduce 95/99th percentile error rates for Dedicated tenants during short bursts by 60% relative to today, under the same capacity envelope.
- Ensure any fallback path is cost-accountable and reversible (no silent charge shifting).
- Provide engineers and SREs a single, observable control to enable/disable tenant escape hatches and to inspect atomic fallback outcomes.
- Keep changes minimally invasive to serving runtime: most of the behavior is routing+policy + small runtime switch.

Non-goals
- This is not a replacement for long-term capacity upgrades or for a full predictive autoscaler. It is complementary to predictive warm pools and burst credits.
- Not attempting to solve model quality regression when switching models; that is addressed separately via evaluation gating (product-optimize).

Design overview
1) Per-tenant Escape Hatch (ETH) - Concept: a tenant-configurable emergency policy that can be triggered automatically (policy) or manually (ops/CS). On trigger, the ETH will do a short-lived set of actions to reduce any tenant's failure surface while preserving key SLAs and accounting.
- Actions available (composable):
  - route X% of traffic to a "safe-lane" model/config (lower-cost or lower-latency model variant)
  - apply per-tenant dynamic rate limit e.g., token-level cap or qps cap for a time window
  - inject graceful 429s with Retry-After and escape-hatch header for clients to surface smarter backoff
  - enable accelerated KV-prefix caching for the tenant to accelerate subsequent requests
- Trigger modes:
  - automatic: threshold-based (queued requests, accelerated error spikes, headroom negative for > T ms)
  - manual: CS / SRE enable via Console or CLI with justification field (audit log)
- Safety gates and accounting:
  - every ETH event creates an immutable audit record and attributed token/CPU charge metrics.
  - escape-hatch window defaults: 30s - 5m, configurable per-tenant.
  - rate-limit and routing decisions honor reserved capacity priorities and do not preempt other tenants.

2) Atomic Fallback primitive (AFP)
- Concept: per-request transactional switch that attempts the primary route and, on pre-defined failure modes or latency violations, retries the same request on a fallback lane atomically (idempotency/side-effect safe by design). The switch is observed as a single logical operation to calling clients (either streaming fallback or a second response).
- Requirements:
  - idempotency/signature: requests must carry a lightweight idempotency envelope or checkpoint (token). For guests without idempotency, we default to non-destructive fallback-only for generation endpoints.
  - bounded retry policy: typically 1 immediate atomic retry to safe-lane; retries should be charge-accounted.
  - latency SLO: AFP adds < 150ms median extra in the 99th percentile worst case vs baseline for atomic retry scenarios.
- Implementation sketch:
  - runtime attempts generate on primary model with a small hard timeout (configurable by route). If timeout or OOM or rate-limited by tenant headroom, collect minimal state (prefix KV pointers, partial logits if applicable) and issue an atomic retry to fallback model/node.
  - the runtime should support a fast state-transfer or canonical re-evaluation path to avoid full re-compute of long prefixes.

Policy interactions and orchestration
- ETH and AFP are complementary: default flow is ETH-enabled tenants will use ETH routing when an automatic ETH event fires; AFP is independent and can be used even when ETH is disabled (AFP is per-request).
- Control plane exposes per-tenant policy: {enable_eth: bool, eth_auto_thresholds: {...}, safe_lane_route: id, enable_afp: bool, afp_retry_budget: integer} (UI representation only; storage in config service).

Operational behaviors and failure modes
- If safe-lane is unavailable, ETH will fall back to controlled throttling (controlled 503/429) with an annotated reason code.
- AFP corner case: if primary request had irreversible side effects and we cannot guarantee idempotency, AFP should not retry by default. API-level flags must be present to opt-in.
- Charge anomalies: ETH-induced routing to cheaper models must still attribute current tenant token usage to tenant billing; any temporary cost differences are recorded in the "escape ledger" for reconciliation.

Observability and SLOs
- New metrics: eth.events.count, eth.duration.histogram, eth.routed_pct per-tenant; afp.attempts, afp.success_on_fallback, afp.latency_overhead.
- Add traces that include a single trace id for atomic-request attempts with annotations for primary-attempt and fallback-attempt.
- Dashboards: per-tenant ETH timeline, global ETH heatmap, AFP success-rate by route/model.
- Alerts: ETH auto-trigger should generate a severity-2 alert to oncall with a link to console to disable event.

Autoscaling tie-ins
- ETH events should be used as soft signals to the autoscaler (not immediate scale-up). When many ETH events target the same pool, autoscaler can: 1) bump warm-pool size, 2) signal prewarm for safe-lane variants, 3) suggest billing/upgrade to tenant owner.
- AFP can be used as a diagnostic input: high afp.success_on_fallback may indicate under-provisioning or model instability.

Runbook (ops) — quick steps
- When ETH auto-triggers for tenant X:
  1) Check console ETH event with reason and recent headroom metrics.
  2) If event persists > 2 windows, run capacity-check: DCD-512 to evaluate short-term reserve or recommend tenant upgrade.
  3) Optionally enable manual extended ETH window with comment.
  4) After resolution, annotate the ETH event and mark as reviewed.
- When AFP has high fallback rate:
  1) Inspect afp.attempts and afp.success_on_fallback for the route; check model logs for OOM/inf-err.
  2) If fallback is because of runtime OOM, escalate to infra with sample request traces.

Migration plan and incremental rollout
- Phase 0 (instrumentation only): add eth.* and afp.* metrics, trace annotations. Feature flags set to off.
- Phase 1 (ops-only): allow SRE/CS to trigger ETH manually from console (no auto mode). Enable AFP for non-side-effect routes only.
- Phase 2 (auto): enable auto-trigger thresholds for a small cohort (10 tenants) with pre-approved CS contacts.
- Phase 3 (wider roll): rollout to all Dedicated tenants with UI controls and tenant-level defaults.

Security, privacy, and compliance considerations
- ETH audit log is immutable; stores who triggered what and why. Logs retain for 365 days by default.
- No tenant traffic is routed to third-party endpoints; safe-lane always runs on Redwood-managed Dedicated nodes aligned with the tenant's region and data isolation constraints.

Open questions / Discussion items
- How to guarantee AFP idempotency for user-provided deterministic functions (e.g., tool-calling)? Do we require caller-provided idempotency tokens?
- Should ETH cost-penalties (if any) be surfaced as preflight warnings to tenants via Console before automatic triggering?
- Do we allow nested ETH (ETH invoking subsumed ETH for sub-tenants / projects)?

Implementation notes (engineering pointers)
- Minimal runtime change: expose a single new RPC path: TryPrimaryThenAtomicFallback(request, policy). This path returns a unified response envelope with annotations.
- Lightweight state capture: store minimal prefix pointers and versioned KV cache keys. Avoid full logits transfer unless necessary.
- Control plane stores per-tenant policy and exposes an audit API.

Next steps and owners
- Proto implementation spike: eng-serving-runtime (Miguel) to validate atomic retry latency with 2 sample models (llama2-13B and a quantized 7B) — deliver perf report by 2025-01-22.
- Console: product (Ava) to add manual ETH toggle and event list by end of Q1.
- SRE: (Liam) to add initial ETH/AFT runbook and pager rules.

Appendix: short example flow (operator view)
- Tenant A starts a rapid fan-out of requests; pool headroom drops and queue grows. Auto-detect triggers ETH: route 30% to safe-lane, cap QPS to 70% of normal, set window = 60s.
- Some requests still hit timeouts; AFP retries those requests on safe-lane and succeeds 90% of the time.
- Observability shows eth.events spike, afp.success_on_fallback climbs. SRE inspects and extends ETH window while autoscaler prewarms safe-lane nodes.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Draft a minimal API schema for the control plane config (one-pager).
- Add a paragraph describing billing reconciliation for escape ledger.
- Validate legal/compliance retention for ETH audit entries.

Comments welcome — this is a rough draft. Ping in #dedicated-product or add inline edits.
